4.3 Design decisions that drive sustainability
4.3.1 Power stage topology and components
• Diode vs. synchronous rectification. The current design uses a Schottky (≈0.2–0.45 V
drop), which is simple and robust but dissipates I × V every cycle. Replacing it with a
f
synchronous MOSFET can cut rectification loss, improving efficiency at medium to

heavy loads and reducing thermal stress extending component life and lowering
embodied impacts from replacements.
• Switch selection. The IRFZ44N’s low R DS is a good starting point. A cooler-running
switch reduces conduction loss I2R shrinking the heatsink/copper area needed and
improving long-term reliability.
• Magnetics and capacitors. The prototype employed ~400 µH inductance and a 50 V
electrolytic output capacitor. Choosing inductors with low DC resistance (Litz or larger
wire gauge) and 105 °C, low-ESR capacitors (or polymer caps where feasible) lowers
ripple and temperature rise—directly improving efficiency and lifetime.
4.3.2 Control strategy and switching frequency
The Arduino-based feedback loop at ~32 kHz is accessible and easily tunable, but the
microcontroller’s quiescent usage and gate-drive style add fixed overhead. A dedicated PWM
controller with low quiescent current can reduce idle draw, while carefully optimizing
frequency trades switching losses against magnetic/capacitor size and ripple. The team’s
demonstrated closed-loop regulation and ripple control form a solid base for such refinement.
4.3.3 Thermal management = longevity
Lower thermal stress extends component lifetime, reducing premature e-waste. Practical steps
include: wide copper pours for heat spreading, short high-di/dt loops, snubbers to tame ringing,
and verifying inductor saturation current with margin. These were already considered in
layout/EMI choices; further optimization compounds both efficiency and reliability gains.
4.4 Sustainable applications (where this boost helps most)
1. High-efficiency DC lighting strings. Boosting to 30–40 V simplifies driving series
LED strings (with a downstream constant-current stage), common in task lighting and
street/area lights. The prototype’s regulated 36–40 V capability and low ripple make it
a suitable front-end for efficient, flicker-free lighting.
2. Battery-backed DC micro-systems. Small DC microgrids, lab benches, or educational
kits can standardize on a 36 V bus for low losses over wiring; the converter raises
modest sources (e.g., 9 V adapters) to that level with measured stability (36.8 V
observed).
3. Edge/IoT instrumentation. Many sensors and actuators are more efficient when
powered from a higher DC rail feeding localized point-of-load regulators. The
converter’s predictable behavior across load steps (overshoot control at light load,
stable at heavy load) supports such use.
Why these are “sustainable”: A higher-voltage DC backbone reduces I²R distribution losses;
efficient conversion minimizes source capacity and storage required; and stable regulation
protects downstream devices, extending their service life—collectively lowering total material
and energy footprints.

4.5 Life-cycle view: materials, manufacturing, and end-of-life
4.5.1 Bill-of-materials hotspots
• Copper and ferrite (inductor): Copper extraction and smelting are energy-intensive;
right-sizing the inductor (avoiding over-design), selecting low-loss cores, and ensuring
adequate saturation current reduce rework and scrap.
• Electrolytic capacitor: Electrolyte dry-out is a common field-failure mode. Selecting
105 °C, long-life, low-ESR parts (or polymer) and keeping them cool extends service
life—fewer replacements mean less material throughput over the product lifetime.
• PCB and solder: Prefer lead-free solder and halogen-free laminates when available.
Good manufacturability (clearances, pad sizing, thermal reliefs) lowers scrap and
rework.
4.5.2 Design for disassembly (DfD)
• Use screws and headers, not glue, for major subassemblies; expose test points; label
parts/values on silkscreen. This makes repair and part harvesting easier. The project’s
use of pluggable headers and screw terminals is aligned with DfD principles.
4.5.3 End-of-life (EoL) guidance
• Mark plastic types and indicate copper weights where possible.
• Provide a one-page EoL sheet: how to depopulate the board, remove the electrolytic
capacitor, and recycle copper-rich magnetics.
• Where regulations apply, conform to RoHS-type substance restrictions and WEEE-
style take-back practices (or the local equivalents).
4.6 Environmental risk reduction through performance tuning
Linking measured behavior to environmental outcomes:
• Ripple control: The prototype already meets a ≤1% ripple target in design and ~0.18–
0.27 V in tests; lowering ripple further can improve LED efficacy and reduce
electromagnetic interference, indirectly saving energy in downstream stages and
minimizing the need for oversized filters.
• Light-load behavior: Addressing the brief overshoot in light-load/near-DCM
transitions (e.g., with slope compensation, adaptive dead-time, or a small preload)
prevents stress on sensitive loads, reducing early-life failures and replacements.
• Thermal headroom: The observed efficiency droop at heavier loads suggests
conduction and thermal losses dominate; incremental improvements lower R
DS(on)
synchronous rectification, tighter loop areas, cooler caps) directly cut waste heat and
extend lifespan.

4.7 Practical roadmap for greener iterations
1. Move to synchronous rectification at the diode position; target ≥2 % absolute
efficiency gain at 0.5 A.
2. Select low-RDC magnetics and verify I ≥ peak current with ≥30% margin to avoid
sat
saturation-induced losses.
3. Adopt 105 °C, low-ESR (or polymer) output caps; validate ripple ≤0.5% under worst
case.
4. Controller optimization: compare Arduino vs. low-Iq controller IC for standby;
measure quiescent draw and step-load response at 32 kHz.
5. Layout refinements: minimize high-di/dt loop area (switch–diode–inductor–cap),
widen power traces, and add snubbers where needed to reduce ringing/EMI (less
radiated energy = less wasted energy).
6. Documentation for repair and EoL: publish a one-page service map (fuse, MOSFET,
diode, inductor, cap locations, test pads), and a recycling note for labs/workshops using
the board.
4.8 Socio-economic context and accessibility
The bill-of-materials selected was cost-aware and locally available, which is critical for
adoption in educational labs and community projects—places where sustainability is as much
about access and maintainability as it is about absolute peak efficiency. The modest cost and
familiar parts (Arduino Nano, IRFZ44N, common Schottky and passives) make repair and
replication feasible, keeping products in service longer and reducing e-waste.
4.9 Summary
The prototype already demonstrates responsible energy conversion—stable 36–40 V
regulation, acceptable ripple, and up to 90% efficiency at mid-load—forming a solid platform
for sustainable deployment. Targeted improvements (synchronous rectification, thermal and
layout tuning, long-life components, and low-Iq control) can abate ~1.4 W of loss at full load
per unit, saving ≈2.1 kWh/year in a typical daily-use scenario, while also extending service life
and easing end-of-life recovery. In applications like efficient DC lighting, small DC
distribution, and robust lab/educational systems, these changes compound into lower operating
energy, fewer replacements, and a lighter environmental footprint—without sacrificing the
accessibility and practicality that made this design succeed in the first place.

Theory:
A single-phase full-wave rectifier with a center-tapped transformer is an AC-to-DC conversion
circuit that makes use of both the positive and negative halves of the input AC signal. The
center-tapped transformer divides the input voltage into two equal and opposite voltages
relative to the center tap, which serves as the reference point. Two diodes are arranged so that
each one conducts during alternating half-cycles of the AC input, resulting in a rectified output
with twice the frequency of the input signal.

Discussion:
This experiment examined the performance of a single-phase full-wave (center-tapped)
rectifier using a resistive load. The input peak-to-peak voltage was measured at 21.20V, while
the output peak-to-peak voltage (Vpp) was 10.20V, resulting in a peak voltage of 10.6V. The
calculated average voltage was 6.7481V, with an RMS voltage of 7.4953V.
The ripple factor, determined to be 48.34%, indicates a moderate level of ripple in the output
signal—characteristic of full-wave rectification, though significantly lower than that of a half-
wave rectifier. The form factor of 1.1107 suggests only slight variation between the RMS and
DC values, confirming that the rectifier delivers a relatively stable DC output.
With an efficiency of 81.06%, the rectifier aligns closely with the theoretical efficiency of a
full-wave rectifier, demonstrating a notable improvement over a half-wave rectifier, which
typically achieves around 40.5% efficiency.
Conclusion:
The experiment successfully validated the expected characteristics of a single-phase full-wave
(center-tapped) rectifier. The output exhibited a moderate ripple factor alongside a high
efficiency of 81.06%. Compared to a half-wave rectifier, the full-wave rectifier provides a more
stable and efficient DC output, making it ideal for applications requiring smoother DC voltage.
While some ripple remains present, implementing additional smoothing techniques, such as
capacitive filtering, could further enhance the output quality.

Abstract

Environmental sustainability has become a critical global concern, with the need to transition
to cleaner energy sources and reduce carbon emissions being more urgent than ever. This report
investigates  the  pivotal  role  of  power  electronics  in  achieving  environmental  sustainability.
Power electronics, involving the efficient conversion, control, and management of electrical
energy, is essential for integrating renewable energy sources, improving energy efficiency, and
enabling sustainable transportation. This report will provide an overview of power electronics,
its key features, and its applications in various sectors. It will also analyse relevant data, discuss
future  prospects,  and  present  a  perspective  on  the  importance  of  power  electronics  in  the
context of Bangladesh's power sector. The findings highlight that power electronics is not just
a technological advancement but a crucial driver for a sustainable future.

Introduction

Global warming, driven by the increasing concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere,
poses a significant threat to the planet. The International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has
confirmed that human activities are the primary cause of the observed warming trend [1]. The
consequences of inaction are severe, including rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and
ecological disruptions. To mitigate these effects, a transition to sustainable energy sources and
the adoption of energy-efficient technologies are imperative.

Sustainable energy, derived from renewable sources like solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal,
offers a viable solution to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels [2]. However, the intermittent
nature of these sources necessitates advanced technologies for efficient energy conversion and
grid integration. Power electronics emerges as a critical technology in this regard. It is the study
and application of solid-state electronics for the conversion and control of electric power. Its
importance lies in its ability to enhance the efficiency of energy use, facilitate the integration
of  renewable  energy  sources,  and  support  the  development  of  sustainable  transportation
systems [3]. Power electronics can withstand high power, with less current consumption, and
controllability.  It  has  been  estimated  that  roughly  15%-20%  of  electricity.  According  to
estimates,  the  extensive  use  of  power  electronics  can  reduce  electricity  consumption  by
between 15 and 20 percent.

This  report  will  delve  into  the  role  of  power  electronics  in  promoting  environmental
sustainability.  It  will  explore  the  key  features  of  power  electronics,  provide  real-world
examples  and  data,  examine  future  trends,  and  discuss  the  specific  implications  for
Bangladesh's power sector.

 Key Features of Power Electronics

Power  electronics  systems  offer  several  key  features  that  contribute  to  environmental
sustainability.

High  Power  Electronics:  Advances  in  high-power  electronics,  particularly  using  wide-
bandgap materials, are revolutionizing the electrical power system. These devices can operate
at  higher  temperatures  and  voltages,  leading  to  increased  efficiency  and  reduced  losses  in
power transmission and distribution.

Energy  Efficiency:  Power  electronics  enables  significant  energy  savings  across  various
applications. By precisely controlling the speed of motors, pumps, and fans, power electronics
optimizes  energy  consumption  in  industrial  processes  and  building  systems.  Hybrid  and
electric  vehicles,  powered  by  power  electronics,  offer  substantial  reductions  in  fuel
consumption and emissions.

Integration  of  Renewable  Energy:  Power  electronics  plays  a  vital  role  in  integrating
intermittent  renewable  energy  sources,  such  as  solar  and  wind,  into  the  electrical  grid  [4].
Power converters adjust the voltage and frequency of renewable energy output to match grid
requirements, ensuring stable and reliable power supply.

Flexible  Control:  Power  electronics  provides  advanced  control  capabilities  for  managing
complex  energy  systems.  This  includes  load  balancing  in  smart  grids,  optimizing  energy
storage, and enabling the integration of distributed generation sources.

More  Flexible  Control  by  Power  Electronics:  Power  electronics  essentially  employs  high-
efficiency switching power semiconductors to convert and control electrical power using dc-
to-dc,  dc-to-ac,  ac-to-dc,  and  ac-to-ac  converters,  which  are  widely  used  in  industrial,
commercial, residential, transportation, aerospace, military, and utility systems.

 Future Scopes

The  future  of  power  electronics  holds  immense  promise  for  advancing  environmental
sustainability.

Next-Generation  Power  Converters:  Research  and  development  efforts  are  focused  on
creating more efficient, compact, and cost-effective power converters. These converters will
play a crucial role in optimizing energy use across various applications, from data centres to
industrial facilities.

Wider Adoption of Electric Aircraft and Green Transportation: The transportation sector
is undergoing a significant transformation with the increasing adoption of electric vehicles and
the development of electric aircraft [7]. Power electronics will continue to be a key enabler of
this transition, driving down emissions and reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

Advanced Grid Technologies: Smart grids will become even more sophisticated, with power
electronics enabling advanced features such as self-healing capabilities, microgrid integration,
and real-time optimization of energy flows.

Materials and Devices: Ongoing research into wide-bandgap semiconductors, such as silicon
carbide  (SiC)  and  gallium  nitride  (GaN),  promises  to  further  enhance  the  efficiency  and
performance of power electronic devices.

Bangladesh Perspective

Bangladesh has recognized the importance of transitioning to cleaner energy sources and has
set ambitious targets for renewable energy adoption. The government aims to generate 40% of
the country's electricity from renewable sources by 2041.

Power electronics will play a crucial role in achieving these goals:

Renewable  Energy  Integration:  Power  electronics  will  be  essential  for  integrating  solar,
wind, and other renewable energy sources into the national grid. This will require investments
in smart grid infrastructure, including advanced power converters, energy storage systems, and
grid management technologies.

Energy  Efficiency  Improvements:  Power  electronics  can  significantly  improve  energy
efficiency in various sectors, including industry, buildings, and transportation. This can help
reduce  electricity  demand,  lower  energy  costs,  and  minimize  the  environmental  impact  of
energy consumption.

Electric  Mobility:  As  Bangladesh  considers  the  adoption  of  electric  vehicles,  power
electronics  will  be  crucial  for  charging  infrastructure,  battery  management,  and  vehicle
propulsion systems.

 Conclusion

Power electronics is a cornerstone technology for achieving environmental sustainability. Its
ability  to  improve  energy  efficiency,  integrate  renewable  energy  sources,  and  enable
sustainable transportation systems makes it an indispensable tool in the global effort to combat
climate change. The data presented in this report underscores the significant impact of power
electronics across various sectors. From smart grids to electric vehicles, power electronics is
driving down emissions, reducing reliance on fossil fuels, and paving the way for a cleaner,
more sustainable future.

In the context of Bangladesh, power electronics offers a pathway to a more sustainable and
resilient  power  sector.  By  embracing  these  technologies  and  investing  in  capacity  building,
Bangladesh  can  accelerate  its  transition  to  cleaner  energy,  improve  energy  access,  and
contribute  to  global  efforts  to  mitigate  climate  change.  The  journey  towards  environmental
sustainability requires collective action, technological innovation, and policy support. Power
electronics stands as a powerful enabler in this journey, offering a brighter, cleaner, and more
sustainable future for all.

Experiment No: 04
Experiment Name: Design and Implementation of a 3-bit Synchronous & Asynchronous

UP/DOWN Counter using Flip-Flops.

Objectives:

1. To understand the basic working principles of synchronous and asynchronous counters and the

fundamental differences between them.

2. To design and implement a 3-bit synchronous Up, Down, and Up-Down counter using T flip-

flops in MATLAB/Simulink or on a digital breadboard.

3. To design and implement a 3-bit asynchronous (ripple) Up, Down, and Up-Down counter

using JK flip-flops.

4. To analyze and compare the propagation delay and timing behavior of synchronous versus

asynchronous counters.

5. To construct the state transition table and timing diagrams for each counter type and verify the

counter sequence experimentally.

6. To evaluate the effect of clock signal on the triggering mechanism of each flip-flop in both

counter configurations.

7. To understand the role of T flip-flops and JK flip-flops in building binary counter circuits and

apply Boolean logic in counter design.

Theory:

A counter is one of the most fundamental and widely used building blocks in digital electronics.

In digital systems, a counter is a sequential circuit that goes through a predefined sequence of states

in response to an input clock signal. Counters are used in a vast array of applications including

frequency division, event counting, digital clocks, timers, memory address generation, and control

sequencing in microprocessors and microcontrollers.

The basic building block of any counter is a flip-flop a bistable multivibrator that can store one bit

of information and change its state in response to a triggering edge (rising or falling) of a clock

signal.  The  most  commonly  used  flip-flops  in  counter  design  are  the  JK  flip-flop  and  the  T

 (Toggle) flip-flop. A T flip-flop toggles its output on every active clock edge when T = 1, while a

JK flip-flop offers SET, RESET, HOLD, and TOGGLE operations based on its J and K inputs.

A  3-bit  binary  counter  uses  three  flip-flops  connected  together  and  counts  from  000  to  111  in

binary (0 to 7 in decimal) for an up counter, or from 111 to 000 for a down counter. An up-down

counter can count in both directions depending on a control input. The sequence of states each flip-

flop output takes constitutes the state transition table of the counter, which is essential for analyzing

its behavior.

There  are  several  types  of  counters  used  in  digital  design:  asynchronous  (ripple)  counters,

synchronous counters, decade counters, ring counters, Johnson counters, up/down counters, and

modulus counters. Each type differs in the way clock pulses are applied, the speed of operation,

and the complexity of design. This experiment focuses on synchronous and asynchronous 3-bit

binary up/down counters.

Asynchronous (Ripple) Counter:

An asynchronous counter, also called a ripple counter, is a type of digital counter in which the flip-

flops do not all share a common clock signal. Instead, only the first flip-flop (least significant bit)

receives the external clock pulse. Each subsequent flip-flop in the chain uses the output Q of the

previous flip-flop as its clock input. As a result, the state change ripples through from one flip-flop

to the next, one at a time hence the name “ripple counter.” Asynchronous counters are typically

built using trailing-edge (negative-edge) triggered JK flip-flops, with J = K = 1 so that each flip-

flop toggles on every falling edge of its clock input. The first flip-flop toggles every clock cycle;

the second toggles every two clock cycles; the third toggles every four clock cycles. This creates

the  standard  binary  counting  sequence.  The  key  advantage  of  the  asynchronous  counter  is  its

simplicity fewer connections and lower hardware complexity. However, because each flip-flop’s

output triggers the next, there is a cumulative propagation delay. In high-speed systems, this delay

can cause glitches and incorrect intermediate states called “spurious states.” For a 3-bit counter, if

the propagation delay per flip-flop is t_pd, the total worst-case delay is 3 × t_pd. This limits the

maximum operating frequency of ripple counters and makes them unsuitable for high-speed or

timing-critical applications.

3-bit Asynchronous Up Counter: In a 3-bit asynchronous up counter, the counter starts at 000

and increments by 1 with each clock pulse, reaching a maximum of 111 (decimal 7) and then

 rolling back to 000. Each flip-flop toggles when the output of the preceding flip-flop transitions

from HIGH to LOW (falling edge). Q0 is the LSB and Q2 is the MSB.

Figure 1: 3-bit Asynchronous Up Counter

3-bit Asynchronous Down Counter: A 3-bit asynchronous down counter counts from 111

(decimal 7) down to 000 and then repeats. In this configuration, each flip-flop is clocked by the

complement output Q̅  of the previous flip-flop rather than Q. This means the next flip-flop

toggles when the previous output transitions from LOW to HIGH, producing a decrementing

binary sequence.

Figure 2: 3-bit Asynchronous Down Counter

3-bit  Asynchronous  Up-Down  Counter:  An  asynchronous  up-down  counter  combines  both

counting  directions  using  a  mode  control  input  (M).  When  M  =  0,  the  counter  counts  up  by

connecting Q outputs to subsequent flip-flop clocks. When M = 1, the counter counts down by

connecting Q̅  outputs instead. Logic gates are used to select the appropriate clock source for each

flip-flop based on the mode input.

Figure 3: 3-bit Asynchronous Up-Down Counter

 Synchronous Counter:

A synchronous counter is a type of digital counter in which all flip-flops share a single common

clock signal. Every flip-flop receives the same clock pulse simultaneously, so their state changes

occur at the same instant. This eliminates the propagation delay problem found in asynchronous

(ripple) counters and allows synchronous counters to operate at much higher clock frequencies. In

a synchronous binary counter, the least significant flip-flop (Q0) always toggles with every clock

pulse. A flip-flop at any higher bit position toggles only when all lower-order bit positions are

simultaneously HIGH (logic 1). This toggling condition is implemented using AND gates whose

inputs are the outputs of all lower-order flip-flops. Synchronous counters are typically designed

using T flip-flops due to the direct relationship between the toggle condition and the carry logic.

The design methodology for a synchronous counter involves creating a state transition table listing

all states and next states, deriving the excitation equations for each flip-flop, and minimizing those

equations using Boolean algebra or Karnaugh maps. The result is a reliable, glitch-free counting

circuit.  Because  all  flip-flops  change  simultaneously,  there  are  no  spurious  intermediate  states,

making synchronous counters the preferred choice in most modern digital system designs.

3-bit  Synchronous  Up  Counter:  In  a  3-bit  synchronous  up  counter,  Q0  always  toggles.  Q1

toggles when Q0 = 1. Q2 toggles when Q0 AND Q1 are both 1. This creates the counting sequence

000 → 001 → 010 → 011 → 100 → 101 → 110 → 111 → 000. AND gates provide the carry

logic for Q1 and Q2.

Figure 4: 3-bit Synchronous Up Counter

3-bit Synchronous Down Counter: In a 3-bit synchronous down counter, Q0 toggles every clock

cycle. Q1 toggles when Q0 = 0 (i.e., Q̅ 0 = 1). Q2 toggles when both Q0 and Q1 are 0. AND gates

on the complemented outputs provide the borrow logic. The counting sequence is 111 → 110 →

101 → 100 → 011 → 010 → 001 → 000 → 111.

 Figure 5: 3-bit Synchronous Down Counter

3-bit  Synchronous  Up-Down  Counter:  The  synchronous  up-down  counter  uses  a  mode

control input M to select between up and down counting. When M = 0, carry logic is derived

from Q outputs. When M = 1, borrow logic is derived from Q̅  outputs. A multiplexer or logic

gate network selects the appropriate enable conditions for each flip-flop based on M, allowing

smooth, simultaneous direction switching without glitches.

Figure 6: 3-bit Synchronous Up-Down Counter

Importance of Synchronous and Asynchronous Counters:

Both  synchronous  and  asynchronous  counters  play  critical  and  complementary  roles  in  digital

system design. Understanding when and why to use each type is essential for any electronics or

mechatronics engineer.

Importance  of  Asynchronous  (Ripple)  Counters:  Asynchronous  counters  are  among  the

simplest  digital  circuits  to  implement.  Their  cascaded  flip-flop  structure  requires  minimal

interconnections  and  fewer  logic  gates,  making  them  cost-effective  and  easy  to  construct,

especially at low operating frequencies.

Importance of Synchronous Counters: Synchronous counters are the backbone of high-speed

digital  systems.  Because  all  flip-flops  are  clocked  simultaneously,  there  is  no  accumulated

propagation  delay,  which  allows  synchronous  counters  to  operate  at  significantly  higher

frequencies  than  asynchronous  ones.  This  makes  them  indispensable  in  modern  processors,

FPGAs, digital signal processors, and high-speed communication systems. Synchronous counters

 also avoid the spurious intermediate states (glitches) that occur in ripple counters, which is crucial

in systems where incorrect transient states could trigger unintended operations.

Comparison Summary: In summary, asynchronous counters are valued for their simplicity and

low-cost  implementation  in  slow,  non-critical  applications,  while  synchronous  counters  are

essential for fast, reliable, and precise digital operations. The choice between the two depends on

the speed requirement, acceptable delay, hardware complexity, and the timing sensitivity of the

target  application. A thorough understanding of  both  counter types gives a digital designer the

flexibility to make optimal design decisions in real-world engineering scenarios.

Discussion:

This experiment involved designing 3-bit synchronous and asynchronous up/down counters using

flip-flops.  The  asynchronous  counter,  built  with  JK  flip-flops,  showed  ripple  delays  due  to

sequential  clocking.  Each  flip-flop  received  its  clock  from  the  previous  stage’s  output,  which

introduced a cumulative propagation delay across the three stages.

Conclusion:

The experiment successfully demonstrated the design and operation of both 3-bit synchronous and

asynchronous up/down counters. Synchronous counters implemented with T flip-flops provided

accurate, glitch-free, and stable outputs by sharing a common clock, making them more reliable

for high-speed applications. Asynchronous counters implemented with JK flip-flops, while simpler

in design, exhibited the characteristic ripple delay that limits their use in timing-critical systems.

Overall,  the  experiment  improved  understanding  of  digital  counter  design,  ff  behavior,  the

comparative timing characteristics of synchronous versus asynchronous sequential circuits.

energy generation, transmission, and utilization one of the greatest engineering challenges of this
century. Power electronics — the conversion and control of electrical power using devices such
as diodes, thyristors, MOSFETs, and IGBTs — has become central to addressing this challenge,
since nearly every stage of a modern power system now passes through some form of electronic
conversion [2]. Beyond traditional motor drives and uninterruptible power supplies, power
electronics is now essential
integrating renewable sources, electric vehicles, HVDC
transmission, and smart grids, all of which depend on converters for voltage regulation,

Key Features of Power Electronics for Sustainability:

Power-electronic converters transfer electricity from one stage of the power system to the next
while allowing its voltage, frequency, and waveform to be flexibly controlled. This flexibility
underlies several features that make power electronics central to environmental and energy
sustainability:

 • Renewable integration: Inverters convert DC output from solar photovoltaic panels and
battery systems, and back-to-back converters regulate variable-frequency wind power,
into stable grid-compatible AC [3].

• Wide-bandgap devices: Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductors
switch faster and operate at higher voltage and temperature than conventional silicon,
cutting conversion losses and reaching efficiencies close to 99 percent [9]–[11].

• Smart-grid and HVDC integration: Power-electronic interfaces allow bidirectional power
flow, voltage regulation, and grid-stability support as more variable renewable capacity is
added.

• Electrification of transport: Traction inverters, on-board chargers, and DC–DC converters
manage power flow between batteries, motors, and charging systems in electric and

Experiment No.: 04
Experiment Name: Study of a Single Acting Cylinder Using Logic IC Gate
Objectives
• To understand the working principle of a single acting pneumatic cylinder.
• To study and apply various logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR).
• To design and implement electro-pneumatic circuits controlled by logic gates.
• To observe how logical inputs control the movement of a single acting cylinder.
• To demonstrate logical decision-making in practical automation systems.
Theory
A single acting pneumatic cylinder is a linear actuator that uses compressed air to move a piston
in one direction—typically to extend. A spring mechanism inside the cylinder returns the piston to
its original position once the air is released. These cylinders usually operate at an air pressure of
80–100 PSI and are commonly controlled with a 3/2-way valve [1].
When compressed air enters the inlet, it pushes the piston forward. When the air is released and
vented, the spring retracts the piston. These cylinders are cost-effective, air-efficient, and ideal for
applications such as clamping, ejecting, or lifting lightweight objects. However, they generate
force in only one direction and are limited by the return spring strength [2].
In pneumatic systems, logical functions can be replicated using air flow and control valves. High
air pressure (flow) represents a logic 1. No air flow (low pressure) represents a logic 0.

• Pneumatic Representation: Two 3/2 valves connected in series. Air passes only if both
valves are open.
• Logical Behavior: Output is 1 only if both inputs are 1.

Discussion
The experiment effectively demonstrated how logic gates can be used to control pneumatic
actuators. Each logic condition was implemented and observed using the De Lorenzo trainer.

A single-phase full-wave rectifier with a center-tapped transformer is an AC-to-DC conversion
circuit that makes use of both the positive and negative halves of the input AC signal. The

Discussion:
This experiment examined the performance of a single-phase full-wave (center-tapped)
rectifier using a resistive load. The input peak-to-peak voltage was measured at 21.20V, while
the output peak-to-peak voltage (Vpp) was 10.20V, resulting in a peak voltage of 10.6V. The

signal—characteristic of full-wave rectification, though significantly lower than that of a half-

efficiency of 81.06%. Compared to a half-wave rectifier, the full-wave rectifier provides a more
stable and efficient DC output, making it ideal for applications requiring smoother DC voltage.
While some ripple remains present, implementing additional smoothing techniques, such as
capacitive filtering, could further enhance the output quality.

Experiment No: 05
Experiment Name: Design and Implementation of SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO, Johnson, Ring
counters in Logisim.
Objectives:
• Understand the fundamental operations of different types of shift registers (SISO, SIPO,
PISO, and PIPO) and counters (Johnson, Ring), as well as their roles in sequential digital
circuits.
• Design logic circuits for each type of shift register and counter using flip-flops and the
required combinational logic components.
• Implement and simulate the designed circuits using Logisim software to verify their
theoretical functionality.
Theory:
A register is a group of flip-flops, each sharing a common clock and capable of storing one bit of
information. An n-bit register consists of a group of n flip-flops capable of storing n bits of binary
information. In addition to the flip-flops, a register may feature combinational gates that perform
specific data-processing tasks. In its broadest definition, a register consists of a group of flip-flops
combined with gates that dictate how information is transferred into the register.
A register capable of shifting its stored binary information to its neighboring cell in a selected
direction is called a shift register. The logical configuration of a shift register consists of a chain
of cascaded flip-flops, with the output of one flip-flop connected to the input of the next. All flip-
flops receive common clock pulses, which activate the shift of data from one stage to the next. [1]
SISO Shift Register:
The SISO shift register is the most basic form of data shifting circuit. It accepts binary data serially
(one bit at a time) through a single input pin and shifts it out serially through a single output pin.
Internally, the output of each flip-flop connects directly to the input of the successive one.
Because data must pass through every single flip-flop in the chain, it requires n clock pulses to
fully load an n-bit word into the register, and another n clock pulses to shift it out completely.
While this makes the SISO register relatively slow for data transfer, it is incredibly useful as a
digital delay line. By adjusting the clock frequency or the number of flip-flops in the cascade,
engineers can introduce a precise time delay into a digital signal, allowing it to act as a
synchronized buffer between asynchronous devices. [2]

Figure 1: SISO Shift Register Logisim circuit diagram
SIPO Shift Register:
The SIPO shift register is primarily used as a serial-to-parallel converter. Like the SISO register,
data is fed into the system serially, bit by bit, requiring n clock cycles to load an n-bit word.
However,  the  key  structural  difference  is  that  the  outputs  of  every  flip-flop  are  externally
accessible simultaneously. Once the entire data string has been clocked into the register, the
complete binary word can be read across the parallel output lines all at once. This configuration is
widely used in communication systems (such as UART receivers) where data is transmitted over
a single wire to save space, but needs to be processed by a microprocessor in parallel chunks (like
8-bit bytes) for faster internal computation. [2]

PISO Shift Register:
The PISO shift register functions as a parallel-to-serial converter, performing the exact opposite
role of the SIPO circuit. It takes parallel data from multiple input lines and transmits it out
sequentially over a single output line. To achieve this, the PISO register utilizes a control signal
typically called "Shift/Load". When this control line is set to the "Load" state, combinational logic
(such as multiplexers) bypasses the shifting mechanism, allowing all n bits of input data to be
jammed into the flip-flops simultaneously on a single clock pulse. Once the data is loaded, the
control line is switched to "Shift", and subsequent clock pulses push the stored data out of the final
flip-flop sequentially. This is a critical component in digital transmitters, taking parallel data from
a computer bus and formatting it for transmission over a single-wire network. [2]

PIPO Shift Register:
The PIPO register is the fastest of the four types because it handles all data loading and outputting
simultaneously. It features dedicated parallel input lines (PI) and parallel output lines (PO). In a
PIPO circuit, there is no physical interconnection between the output of one flip-flop and the input
of the next; therefore, no actual "shifting" of data occurs between the internal cells. Instead, upon
the arrival of the clock edge, the data present on the input lines is instantly transferred to the output
lines in a single clock cycle. This configuration acts as a multi-bit data latch, serving as temporary
memory  storage  or  a  synchronization  buffer  holding  data  steady  while  other  parts  of  a
microprocessor complete their operations. [2]

Johnson Counter
A Johnson Counter (also known as a Twisted Ring Counter) is an advanced variation of a shift
register where the inverted output (Q-bar or complemented output) of the final flip-flop is fed back
into the data input of the first flip-flop. Because of this twisted feedback loop, an n-stage Johnson
counter cycles through exactly 2n distinct states before repeating. For example, a 4-bit Johnson
counter will produce 8 unique states. The sequence fills with 1s from left to right, and then empties
with 0s from left to right. This behavior requires significantly less decoding logic than a traditional
binary counter. As a result, Johnson counters are highly favored in hardware design for creating
complex  timing  sequences,  multi-phase  clock  generators,  and  glitch-free  digital  frequency
dividers.

Ring Counter:
A Ring Counter is a straightforward circular shift register where the standard, non-inverted output
(Q) of the last flip-flop is looped directly back to the input of the first flip-flop. Unlike the Johnson
counter, a Ring counter typically requires a pre-set or initialization step where a single logic '1' is
injected into the first flip-flop while the rest are set to '0'. Once the clock starts, this single '1' simply
rotates endlessly through the chain of flip-flops. Because only one output is high at any given
moment, an n-bit ring counter provides n distinct states. This "one-hot" state encoding makes the
Ring Counter exceptionally easy to decode, eliminating the need for external logic gates when
stepping through a specific sequence of operations in a microcontroller or state machine. [2]

Discussion:
In this experiment, different types of shift registers including SISO, SIPO, PISO, and PIPO—along
with Ring Counter and Johnson Counter circuits, were designed and simulated using Logisim. The
shift registers demonstrated various methods of data storage and transfer through serial and parallel
input-output configurations controlled by clock pulses. The SISO and SIPO registers successfully
illustrated the conversion of serial data into serial and parallel outputs, respectively. Conversely,
the PISO and PIPO registers demonstrated the handling of parallel data with serial or parallel
outputs. Additionally, the Ring Counter exhibited the circulation of a single logic state through a
sequence of flip-flops, whereas the Johnson Counter generated a unique counting sequence by
feeding the inverted output of the last flip-flop back to the first. The simulation results for all
circuits were consistent with their theoretical operations, firmly verifying the correctness of the
designs.
Conclusion:
This experiment provided valuable insight into the operation and practical applications of shift
registers and counters in digital electronics. Through Logisim simulation, the principles of data
storage, data shifting, and sequence generation were successfully demonstrated. The behavior of
the SISO, SIPO, PISO, and PIPO shift registers, as well as the Ring and Johnson Counters,
perfectly matched the expected theoretical outcomes. This successfully fulfills the objectives of
the experiment and strengthens our foundational understanding of sequential logic systems.

Introduction:
The ATmega32 is an 8-bit AVR microcontroller based on a modified Harvard architecture. It has
separate memories for program and data, which allows faster instruction execution. ATmega32 provides
four 8-bit I/O ports: PORTA, PORTB, PORTC, and PORTD. Each port has: A Data Direction Register
(DDRx) to configure input or output. A PORTx register to write output values. A PINx register to read
inputs. In this experiment, PORTC was used as an output port to drive eight LEDs. Each bit of PORTC
corresponds to one LED [1]. Writing logic 1 turns an LED ON, and writing logic 0 turns it OFF. A
delay was introduced using the _delay_ms() function to make the blinking pattern visible to the human
eye [1].

**Objectives:**

1. To configure the Atmega32 microcontroller for generating a 1Hz signal using Timer0.
2. To simulate the 1Hz signal generation using Proteus software.
3. To understand the process of setting up Timer0 on the Atmega32.
4. To verify the accuracy and stability of the generated 1Hz signal through simulation.
5. To demonstrate the practical application of microcontroller timers in signal generation.

**Theory:**

Timers are integral peripherals in microcontrollers used for counting and timing applications. The Atmega32 microcontroller features several timers, including Timer0, an 8-bit timer. The timer can be configured to operate in various modes, such as Normal, CTC (Clear Timer on Compare Match), Fast PWM, and Phase Correct PWM. To generate a 1Hz signal, the CTC mode of Timer0 can be used. In CTC mode, the timer counter (TCNT0) counts from 0 to a specified value stored in the Output Compare Register (OCR0). When the counter matches the OCR0 value, it resets to 0 and an interrupt can be triggered.

In AVR ATmega16 / ATmega32, there are three timers:

* **Timer0**: 8-bit timer
* **Timer1**: 16-bit timer
* **Timer2**: 8-bit timer

Basic registers and flags of the Timers:

**TCNTn (Timer / Counter Register):** Every timer has a timer/counter register. It is zero upon reset. It counts up with each clock pulse.

**TOVn (Timer Overflow Flag)**: Each timer has a Timer Overflow flag. When the timer overflows, this flag will get set.

**TCCRn (Timer Counter Control Register)**: This register is used for setting the modes of timer/counter.

**OCRn** (**Output Compare Register):** The value in this register is compared with the content of the TCNTn register. When they are equal, the OCFn flag will get set.

**<u>Timer0:</u>**

**TCNT0 (Timer / Counter Register 0)**: It is an 8-bit register. It counts up with each pulse.

**TCCR0 (Timer / Counter Control register 0)**: This is an 8-bit register used for the operation mode and the clock source selection [1].

**Timer0 Overflow**

Normal mode: When the counter overflows i.e. goes from 0xFF to 0x00, the TOV0 flag is set.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64...)

*Figure- 8.1: Timer0 Overflow* [2]*.*

In this experiment, the aim is to be generated a 1Hz signal using the Atmega32 microcontroller and its Timer0 module, simulated in the Proteus environment. The goal is to understand the working of timers in microcontrollers and to demonstrate how to configure them to achieve specific timing tasks.

**Working Principle:**

1. The code set was set all of PORTC's pins to output and initialized Timer0 to cause an interrupt upon overflow.
2. Timer0 was set up to run in Normal Mode with a 64-bit prescaler and enabled global interrupts.
3. After that, the main program was into an endless loop.
4. The ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) was triggered when Timer0 overflows, increasing the value of the ovf count variable.
5. Toggling the value of PORTC was occured when ovf\_count reached 61, or around one second with a prescaler of 64. To resume counting after toggling, ovf count is reset to 0.

* **System Clock (F\_CPU):** 1 MHz
* **Prescaler:** 64(Assume)
* The timer clock frequency is**\_**

$$TCF=\frac{F (CPU)}{Prescaler}$$

So, for a 1MHz system clock with 64 prescaler.

$$TCF=\frac{1000000}{64}=15625 Hz$$

* The period of one timer tick (the time it takes for the timer to increment by one) is the Timer Tick Period.

$$TTP=\frac{1 }{15625}=64×10^{-6} sec$$

* As this timer0 has 8 bits the timer counts from 0 to 255, it overflows every 256 counts.

$$Overflow Period=256×\left(64×10^{-6} \right)=16.384×10^{-3} sec$$

* Thus, the timer overflows approximately every 16.384\*10^-3 sec with a prescaler of 64. Now to generate a 1Hz signal, here need an interrupt to occur every 1 sec. Since each overflow occurs every 16.384\*10^-3 sec.

$$Number of Overflows= \frac{1}{16.384×10^{-3}}=61$$

Approximately 61 overflows are required to achieve 1 sec. Thus, by counting the number of overflows, a pin is toggled to generate a 1 Hz signal.

**Required Components:**

1. Atmega32 Microcontroller.
2. Push button.
3. LED
4. Resistors

**Code:**

#include <avr/io.h>

#include <avr/interrupt.h>

volatile *uint8\_t* ovf\_count=0;

int main(void)

{

DDRC=0xFF;

TIMSK |= 0x01;

TCNT0= 0;

TCCR0= 0x03;

//enable global interrupt(bit7 of SREG)

sei();

while (1)

{

}

}

//Timer0 overflow interrupt service routine

ISR(TIMER0\_OVF\_vect)

{

ovf\_count= ovf\_count + 1;

//61 required to get 1 sec

if(ovf\_count == 61)

{

PORTC ^= 0xFF;

//reset counter

ovf\_count = 0;

}

}

2. **Periodic Interrupts:** Useful in scheduling tasks in real-time systems.

The experiment successfully demonstrated the generation of a 1Hz signal using the Atmega32 microcontroller's Timer0. **Theory:**

A servomotor (or servo motor or simply servo) is a rotary or linear actuator that allows for precise control of angular or linear position, velocity, and acceleration in a mechanical system. It constitutes part of a servomechanism, and consists of a suitable motor coupled to a sensor for position feedback and a controller (often a dedicated module designed specifically for servomotors). Servomotors are not a specific class of motor, although the term servomotor is often used to refer to a motor suitable for use in a closed-loop control system. Servomotors are used in applications such as robotics, CNC machinery, and automated manufacturing. servomotor is a closed-loop servomechanism that uses position feedback (either linear or rotational position) to control its motion and final position. The input to its control is a signal (either analog or digital) representing the desired position of the output shaft.

The motor is paired with some type of position encoder to provide position feedback (and potentially also speed feedback in more sophisticated designs). The controller compares the measured position with the desired position to generate an error signal, which when fed back causes the motor to rotate in the direction needed to bring the shaft to the desired position. The error signal reduces to zero as the desired position is approached, stopping the motor.

![How to drive servo motor control with AVR microcontroller - Do It Easy With  ScienceProg](data:image/jpeg;base64...)![Servo Motor SG90 - Robotech BD - Servo Motor SG90 %](data:image/png;base64...)

Commonly, servos are electric, hydraulic, or pneumatic. They operate on the principle of negative feedback, where the control input is compared to the actual position of the mechanical system as measured by some type of transducer at the output. The position loop regulates the position of the motor or system. In Position mode control, feedback such as an encoder or resolver ensures that the actual position is equal to the commanded position [2].

This experiment demonstrates the control of a servo motor using an Atmega32 microcontroller. The microcontroller generates PWM signals that control the position of the servo motor. The provided code initializes the microcontroller's PWM functionality and adjusts the duty cycle to move the servo to specific angles.

**Working Principle:**

1. Firstly, PD5 was configured as an output pin to send the PWM signal to the servo motor.
2. Timer1 was set up in Fast PWM mode with ICR1 as the TOP value to generate a PWM signal with a 20ms period (50Hz frequency). The prescaler was set to 8.
3. The initial pulse width was set to 1.2ms, positioning the servo at approximately 0 degrees.
4. The OCR1A was adjusted register changes the pulse width:
   1. 600 (0.6ms): ~-90 degrees
   2. 900 (0.9ms): ~-45 degrees
   3. 1200 (1.2ms): 0 degrees
   4. 1500 (1.5ms): +45 degrees
   5. 1800 (1.8ms): +90 degrees
5. The loop cycles through different pulse widths, causing the servo motor to move to different positions. Each position was held for 2 seconds before moving to the next position.
6. The servo motor's shaft position was controlled by the width of the PWM pulse, which was set by the OCR1A register. The changes in OCR1A values result in different pulse widths, thereby moving the servo to the desired angles.

CHAPTER 1: APPLYING POWER ELECTRONICS KNOWLEDGE
1.1 Introduction
Power electronics plays a fundamental role in modern electrical and electronic systems, enabling
efficient conversion, regulation, and control of power. Among the DC–DC converter topologies,
the boost converter is particularly significant due to its ability to step up low voltages to higher
regulated levels. Applications range from renewable energy integration to portable devices and
automotive systems [1]. This project, titled “Design and Implementation of a 5V to 16V DC–DC
Boost Converter Using Arduino-Based PWM Control”, bridges classroom knowledge with real-
world application.
1.2 Relevance of Power Electronics in the Project
Typical 5 V sources such as USB ports, microcontrollers, or battery packs are insufficient to
directly power 12–16 V loads like LED arrays, sensors, or embedded controllers. A boost converter
efficiently raises the voltage while ensuring compactness and stability [2]. This project applies
concepts including duty cycle control, energy storage in inductors and capacitors, and PWM-
driven switching devices to achieve regulation.
1.3 Theory of Boost Converter
A boost (step-up) DC–DC converter transfers energy from an input source to a higher output
voltage using an inductor, a controlled switch, a diode (or synchronous rectifier), and an output
capacitor.
• ON Interval: The MOSFET switch is closed, allowing the inductor to store energy as its
current ramps upward. The diode is reverse-biased, and the output capacitor supplies the
load.
• OFF Interval: The MOSFET is opened, the inductor current flows through the diode into
the capacitor and load, boosting the output voltage above the input.
In continuous conduction mode (CCM), the ideal conversion ratio is:

In practice, efficiency is reduced by MOSFET conduction losses, diode forward drop, inductor
copper/core losses, and capacitor ESR. These non-idealities slightly increase the required duty
cycle compared to the theoretical value.
For regulation, a voltage-mode control loop is typically used. In this project, the output voltage
was sensed through a resistive divider, digitized by the Arduino ADC, and compared against a
reference. The Arduino then adjusted the PWM duty cycle to stabilize the output at ~16 V. Higher-
frequency PWM (e.g., using Timer2 at ~62.5 kHz) was applied to reduce audible noise and output
ripple [3].

CHAPTER 2: DESIGNING ENGINEERING SOLUTIONS
2.1 Introduction
Engineering solutions transform theoretical knowledge into practical hardware. This chapter
details  the  systematic  design  of  the  Arduino-controlled  boost  converter,  including  analysis,
simulation, circuit design, coding, and hardware prototyping.
2.2 Design Specifications
The main technical requirements for the boost converter are summarized below:
•  Input voltage: 5 V (USB/battery source).
•  Target output voltage: 16 V regulated.
•  Regulation tolerance: ±0.2 V.
•  Estimated duty cycle: ~69%.
•  Switching device: N-channel MOSFET driven by Arduino PWM.
•  Feedback path: Voltage divider (8 kΩ / 1 kΩ) scaled down output for ADC input.
•  Control method: Closed-loop PWM with deadband to prevent oscillations.

2.5 Methodology
We can divide the methodology into four key sections.
2.5.1 Theoretical Analysis
• Required duty cycle ≈ 69%.
• Minimum inductance and capacitance estimated to ensure continuous conduction mode
(CCM).
2.5.2 Circuit Design
• MOSFET as switching device.
• Diode for current freewheeling.
• Inductor and capacitor for energy storage and filtering.
• Voltage divider connected to Arduino pin A5 for feedback.
2.5.3 Control Strategy
• Arduino pin 11 outputs PWM to drive MOSFET.
• Timer2 register modified to increase PWM frequency and reduce audible noise.
• Feedback compared against a set reference to adjust duty cycle dynamically.
2.5.4 Arduino Code
const int feedback = A5;
const int PWM = 11;
int pwm = 40;
const int desiredFeedback = 347;
const int pwmMin = 30;
const int pwmMax = 60;
const int deadband = 5;
unsigned long lastUpdate = 0;
const unsigned long updateInterval = 10;
void setup() {
pinMode(feedback, INPUT);
pinMode(PWM, OUTPUT);
TCCR2B = (TCCR2B & B11111000) | B00000001;
analogWrite(PWM, pwm);
}
void loop() {
unsigned long now = millis();
if (now - lastUpdate >= updateInterval) {
lastUpdate = now;
int actualFeedback = analogRead(feedback);
if (actualFeedback < desiredFeedback - deadband) {

pwm = constrain(pwm + 1, pwmMin, pwmMax);
} else if (actualFeedback > desiredFeedback + deadband) {
pwm = constrain(pwm - 1, pwmMin, pwmMax);
}
analogWrite(PWM, pwm);
}
}
2.6 WORKING PRINCIPLE
• Step-up conversion was achieved by storing energy in the inductor during the ON interval
and delivering it through the diode during the OFF interval, yielding Vout > Vin (5 V →
~16 V).
• The power stage was realized with an inductor, a PWM-driven MOSFET switch, a diode,
an output capacitor, and an 8 kΩ / 1 kΩ divider that fed the Arduino ADC for voltage
feedback.
• During the ON phase, the MOSFET was turned ON, the diode was reverse-biased, the
inductor current ramped upward with VL ~ +Vin, and the output capacitor supported the
load.
• During the OFF phase, the MOSFET was turned OFF, the inductor voltage swung negative
(VL ~ Vin − Vout < 0), forcing current through the diode into the output capacitor and
load, thereby boosting the output.
• Regulation was maintained by adjusting the PWM duty cycle; in ideal CCM the static
relation Vout = Vin / (1 − D) was followed, while non-ideal losses required a slightly higher
effective duty cycle.
• Output voltage was sensed through the 8 kΩ / 1 kΩ divider (~1:9), presenting ~1.78 V to
the ADC at Vout = 16 V and enabling closed-loop control under input and load variations.
• In this build, inductors of 200 µH + 200 µH + 100 µH were connected in series to realize
~500 µH total inductance, keeping current ripple manageable at the chosen switching
frequency.

CHAPTER 3: CONTEXTUAL REASONING IN POWER ELECTRONICS
3.1 Introduction
Power electronic design must balance theoretical expectations with real-world constraints such as
load variations, thermal effects, and efficiency. The performance of a boost converter is measured
by its ability to maintain a stable output, minimize ripple, and operate efficiently across different
loads. This chapter evaluates the performance of the Arduino-controlled 5 V to 16 V boost
converter, focusing on measurement setup, results, comparison with theory, limitations, and design
trade-offs.
3.2 Measurement Setup
To assess performance, both no-load and variable load conditions were tested.
• Input Source: 5 V regulated supply (USB/battery).
• Load: Potentiometer adjustable between 1 kΩ and 100 kΩ.
• Measuring Instruments:
Digital Multimeter for voltage readings.
Oscilloscope for PWM and ripple observation (where available).
• Feedback Path: An 8 kΩ / 1 kΩ divider scaled down the output to ~1.78 V at 16 V,
allowing Arduino ADC to regulate PWM duty cycle.
3.3 Results
We found the following results.
3.3.1 No-Load Performance
• Input: 5 V
• Output: 16.0 V (±0.2 V)
• Ripple: Negligible, within acceptable tolerance.
3.3.2 Variable Load Performance
• Load range: 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ
• Output voltage remained within 15.8 V – 16.2 V
• Ripple slightly increased under heavy load but stayed acceptable.
3.3.3 Efficiency Estimate
The converter achieved an estimated efficiency of 85–90%, based on measured voltage stability
and thermal behavior. Minor losses were due to MOSFET conduction resistance, diode forward
drop, and inductor resistance.
3.4 Comparison with Theoretical Analysis
From design calculation:

The theoretical output was 16 V at ~69% duty cycle. The experimental value of 16.0 V (±0.2 V)
closely matched the theoretical prediction. Variations arose from real-world non-idealities
including ESR of capacitors, inductor winding resistance, and switching losses. This confirmed
that the system achieved the intended design goals.
3.5 Limitations of the Design
Despite successful operation, the following limitations were observed:
• PWM Frequency: Arduino-generated PWM was limited to tens of kHz, constraining
efficiency compared to dedicated controllers.
• Breadboard Parasitics: Prototyping on a breadboard introduced extra resistance and
inductance.
• Thermal Effects: At lower load resistances, MOSFET heating was noticeable.
• Ripple: Although acceptable, ripple could be further minimized by optimizing filter
capacitor selection.
3.6 Discussion
The closed-loop feedback path proved crucial in maintaining stable output voltage under both no-
load and load conditions. By dynamically adjusting the duty cycle, the system corrected deviations
and avoided overshoot. Compared to open-loop operation, this resulted in tighter regulation and
improved robustness [4]. The ±0.2 V fluctuation observed was within acceptable limits and
demonstrated that the converter operated reliably in practice.
3.7 Summary
This chapter provided a detailed evaluation of the converter’s performance. The system
successfully boosted 5 V to 16.0 V with ±0.2 V fluctuation, showing excellent stability across
varying load conditions. The results matched theoretical predictions, validating the design.
Limitations such as breadboard parasitics and PWM frequency constraints were noted, guiding
future improvements.

CHAPTER 4: SUSTAINABLE APPLICATIONS AND ENVIRONMENTAL
IMPACT
4.1 Introduction
Sustainability is a key consideration in modern engineering. Boost converters enhance efficiency,
reduce energy losses, and support renewable energy systems. This chapter outlines the sustainable
applications and environmental impact of the designed converter.
4.2 Sustainable Applications
4.2.1 Integration with Renewable Energy Sources
i. Solar panels and micro wind turbines often generate low, fluctuating voltages. Boost
converters enable these sources to power higher-voltage loads or charge batteries [5].
ii. In off-grid systems, regulated DC outputs from boost converters increase the usability of
renewable sources.
4.2.2 Battery-Powered and Portable Devices
i. Boost converters extend battery usability by stepping up nominal voltages to required load
levels.
ii. This reduces reliance on multiple batteries, conserving resources.
4.2.3 LED Lighting and Smart Electronics
LEDs are highly energy-efficient lighting sources, but many LED systems require 12–16 V
operation. By stepping up 5 V to 16 V efficiently, the boost converter allows low-voltage USB or
battery supplies to power LEDs, supporting the global transition toward sustainable lighting
solutions.
4.2.4 Educational and Low-Cost Prototyping
The use of an Arduino-based digital control system makes the converter accessible for students
and engineers at low cost. This encourages sustainable education by promoting the reuse of
microcontrollers and standard components in multiple projects rather than single-purpose
hardware.
4.3 Environmental Impact
4.3.1 Energy Efficiency
The developed boost converter achieved ~90–95% efficiency, ensuring that only a small portion
of input energy is wasted as heat. High-efficiency power electronics directly translate into energy
savings and reduced demand from the power grid.

4.3.2 Minimizing Electronic Waste
By using off-the-shelf, widely available components (Arduino, MOSFET, Schottky diode,
electrolytic capacitors), the project demonstrates that functional prototypes can be built without
relying on highly specialized or single-use components. This promotes reusability and reduces
electronic waste generation.
4.3.3 Support for Green Energy Transition
Efficient power converters are indispensable for scaling up renewable energy integration. Boost
converters ensure that low-voltage renewable sources can reliably contribute to practical energy
systems, helping reduce reliance on fossil fuels and lowering carbon emissions [6].
4.3.4 Future Sustainable Improvements
Future iterations of the design could incorporate:
i. Synchronous rectification instead of Schottky diodes to further reduce conduction losses.
ii. Optimized PCB layouts for reduced parasitic losses and improved thermal management.
iii. RoHS-compliant and recyclable components, reducing environmental impact over the life
cycle of the product.
4.4 Summary
Boost converters contribute directly to sustainable engineering by improving energy efficiency,
reducing waste, and enabling renewable integration. The designed system supports both technical
performance and environmental goals.

 Experiment No.: 06
Experiment Name: Implementation of Basic Logic Gates Using Integrated Circuits (ICs) on
Breadboard.

Objectives:

•  To comprehend the operational principles and truth tables of fundamental digital logic
gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR) through practical hardware
implementation.

•  To implement, verify, and analyze the circuit behavior of these basic logic gates utilizing

standard TTL ICs on a prototyping breadboard.

•  To cultivate essential hands-on skills in digital circuit wiring, component integration, and

the troubleshooting of connectivity issues.

•  To bridge the theoretical-practical divide by directly correlating theoretical Boolean logic

design with tangible, physical outputs.

Introduction:

Digital  electronics  form  the  bedrock  of  modern  computing,  communication,  and  control
architectures. At the core of these systems  are logic gates, which  are the fundamental  building
blocks  that  execute  basic  Boolean  operations  required  for  sophisticated  electronic  design.  To
effectively  bridge  theoretical  logic  concepts  with  real-world  applications,  practical  circuit
implementation is strictly necessary.

This experiment investigates the operation of the primary logic gates (7408 (AND), 7432 (OR),
7404  (NOT),  7400  (NAND),  7402  (NOR),  7486(XOR),  74266(XNOR))  using  74-series
Transistor-Transistor Logic (TTL) integrated circuits. The TTL ICs utilized in this lab encapsulate
multiple independent logic gates within a single package. By physically wiring these components
on  a  breadboard,  applying  +5V  DC  regulated  power,  and  monitoring  output  states  via  LED
indicators, theoretical truth tables are empirically verified. This hands-on methodology not only
demonstrates the functional realities of digital logic but also establishes a foundational skill set for
designing  more  complex  architectures  like  arithmetic  logic  units  (ALUs),  multiplexers,  and
memory registers.

In  this  laboratory  experiment,  these  logic  gates  are  implemented  and  tested  on  a  breadboard,
allowing circuit construction without permanent soldering. This hands-on approach helps students
understand the practical operation of logic gates and their role in building larger digital systems
such as multiplexers, adders, and flip-flops. The output of each gate is displayed using an LED
connected  through  a  current-limiting  resistor,  while  a  regulated  +5  V  DC  supply  provides  the
operating  voltage  required  for  TTL  devices.  Jumper  wires  are  used  to  establish  the  necessary
circuit  connections  between  the  ICs,  power  source,  and  ground.  Through  the  successful
implementation  and  testing  of  these  logic  gates,  students  gain  practical  experience  in  circuit
assembly, verification, and troubleshooting. These skills form an essential foundation for advanced
studies in digital electronics, microprocessor systems, and embedded system design.

 Required Apparatus

1.  Breadboard
2.  +5V DC Power Supply
3.  Digital TTL Logic ICs: IC 7408 (Quad 2-Input AND Gate), IC 7432 (Quad 2-Input OR
Gate), IC 7404 (Hex Inverter/NOT Gate), IC 7400 (Quad 2-Input NAND Gate), IC 7402
(Quad 2-Input NOR Gate), IC 7486 (Quad 2-Input XOR Gate), IC 74266 / IC 4077
(Quad 2-Input XNOR Gate)

4.  Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) (7 pcs)
5.  Current-Limiting Resistors
6.  Input Push Buttons (2 pcs)
7.  Jumper Wires (As required)

Working Procedure

1.  Preparation:  All  necessary  hardware,  including  the  breadboard,  specified  TTL  ICs,
resistors,  LEDs,  jumper  wires,  and  the  +5V  DC  power  supply,  was  assembled  and
inspected.

2.  Component  Mounting:  The  selected  logic  ICs  were  firmly  mounted  across  the  central
divider of the breadboard to ensure electrical isolation between the opposing rows of pins.
3.  Power Distribution (Biasing): To activate the logic chips, the VCC and GND terminals of
each  IC  were  wired  directly  to  the  +5V  rail  and  the  common  ground  rail,  respectively,
establishing the necessary operating voltage.

4.  Input Configuration: Push-button switches were integrated into the circuit and connected
to the gate inputs, serving as manual generators to toggle logic states between HIGH and
LOW.

5.  Output Monitoring: LEDs, placed in series with $220~\Omega$ current-limiting resistors,
were connected to the respective output pins of the logic gates to safely visualize the signal
status.

6.  Testing  and  Simulation:  The  input  switches  were  methodically  toggled  to  simulate  all

possible binary combinations outlined in the standard truth tables.

7.  Data Collection and Verification: The resulting output responses for the AND, OR, NOT,
NAND,  NOR,  XOR,  and  XNOR  gates  were  observed  via  the  LEDs,  documented,  and
cross-referenced against theoretical expectations to verify accurate gate functionality.
8.  Teardown:  Following  successful  verification,  the  power  supply  was  isolated,  and  the

breadboard circuit was carefully dismantled.

Circuit Development

1. AND Gate (IC 7408): The AND gate executes the Boolean multiplication operation (Y = A.
B).  It  dictates  that  the  output  will  register  as  HIGH  (1)  strictly  when  all  individual  inputs  are
simultaneously HIGH. Conversely, if any single input is LOW (0), the output is driven LOW. This
logic is widely applied in decision-making circuits where multiple conditions must be met. The IC
7408 serves this function, providing four independent 2-input AND gates in one package.

 Figure 6.1: Basic NOR Gate

2. OR Gate (IC 7432): The OR gate performs Boolean addition (Y = A + B). It yields a HIGH
(1) output if at least one of its inputs is actively HIGH. The output drops to LOW (0) only when
every  input  is  LOW.  This  behavior  is  utilized  in  systems  where  independent  conditions  can
individually trigger a shared output response. The IC 7432 is standard for this operation, containing
four 2-input OR gates.

Fig 2: OR Gate

3.  NOT  Gate  (IC  7404):  Commonly  termed  an  inverter,  the  NOT  gate  performs  logical
complementation. Featuring a single input and single output, it simply reverses the logic state: a
HIGH input yields a LOW output, and a LOW input yields a HIGH output. It is heavily relied
upon for signal inversion and logic control. The 7404 IC provides six discrete NOT gates.

Fig 03: NOT Gate

 4. NAND Gate (IC 7400): The NAND (NOT-AND) gate is a universal logic element that produces
a LOW (0) output exclusively when  all inputs  are HIGH (1); otherwise, it  defaults to  a HIGH
output.  Functionally,  it  operates  as  an  AND  gate  immediately  followed  by  an  inverter.  Its
"universal" designation stems from the fact that any digital logic circuit can be synthesized using
NAND gates alone. The IC 7400 contains four independent 2-input NAND gates.

Fig 4: NAND Gate

5. NOR Gate (IC 7402): The NOR (NOT-OR) gate is the second universal logic gate, outputting
a HIGH signal solely when all inputs are held LOW. Any presence of a HIGH input immediately
forces the output LOW. Like the NAND gate, it can be configured to replicate the function of any
other digital gate. The IC 7402 facilitates this with four independent 2-input NOR gates.

Fig 5: NOR Gate

6. XOR Gate (IC 7486): The Exclusive-OR (XOR) gate serves as a digital inequality detector. It
generates a HIGH (1) output only when its inputs are at differing logic levels (e.g., one HIGH, one
LOW).  If  the  inputs  match,  the  output  is  LOW.  This  characteristic  makes  it  indispensable  for
binary  arithmetic  addition,  parity  generation,  and  error  detection.  The  7486  IC  contains  four
independent 2-input XOR gates.

Fig 6: XOR Gate

 7.XNOR Gate (IC 74266 / IC 4077): The Exclusive-NOR (XNOR) gate acts as an equivalence
or equality detector. It produces a HIGH (1) output when its inputs are identical (both HIGH or
both LOW), and a LOW (0) output when the inputs diverge. Acting as the precise inverse of the
XOR gate, it is highly utilized in data verification and digital comparison systems.

Discussion

Fig 7: XNOR Gate

Throughout this laboratory exercise, the core logic behaviors of AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR,
XOR,  and  XNOR  gates  were  successfully  and  empirically  validated  utilizing  standard  TTL
integrated circuits. The implementation required meticulous attention to breadboard architecture,
specifically regarding proper IC placement across the central trench and accurate pin-to-pin wiring.
The standard 74-series ICs utilized feature durable outer plastic housings with standardized pin
numbering, which greatly streamlined the identification and prototyping process.

By employing tactile push buttons to inject logic signals and LEDs to visually monitor the resulting
output  states,  the  physical  hardware  behavior  was  proven  to  align  flawlessly  with  established
theoretical  Boolean  truth  tables.  The  accuracy  of  these  results  was  highly  dependent  on
maintaining a stable +5V DC power supply, ensuring correct VCC and GND biasing for every
chip, and adhering strictly to the pin diagrams. Ultimately, this exercise underscored the reliability
of TTL ICs as the foundational architecture for complex digital electronics and highlighted the
necessity of systematic troubleshooting in hardware development.

Conclusion

This  experiment  successfully  fulfilled  all  stated  objectives  by  demonstrating  the  operational
dynamics  of  fundamental  digital  logic  gates  through  direct  hardware  implementation.  The
empirical verification of the truth tables for the AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, and XNOR
gates  confirmed  absolute  alignment  between  theoretical  Boolean  logic  and  physical  circuit
behavior. Furthermore, the hands-on methodology cultivated essential practical engineering skills,
including prototyping, component integration, and systematic troubleshooting, providing a robust
conceptual and practical foundation for future studies in advanced digital system design.

Introduction:
Digital  logic  gates  are  the  fundamental  building  blocks  of  digital  electronics  and  computer
systems.  Among  all  logic  gates,  the  NAND  gate  holds  special  importance  because  it  is  a
universal gate, meaning that any other logic gate or digital circuit can be constructed using only
NAND  gates  [1].  Microcontrollers  such  as  the  ATmega32  provide  a  flexible  platform  for
implementing digital logic functions through software, eliminating the need for discrete logic
ICs and  enabling rapid  prototyping [2].  In this experiment,  an ATmega32 microcontroller is
used to implement a NAND gate by reading two digital inputs from push-button switches and
producing  the  corresponding  output  on  an  LED.  The  logic  operation  is  performed
programmatically inside the microcontroller, demonstrating the use of embedded systems for
digital logic realization.

Theory:
 A NAND gate performs the logical NOT of the AND operation. The ATmega32 is an 8-bit AVR
microcontroller featuring 32 programmable I/O pins, which can be configured as either inputs
or outputs through software registers [2]. By reading the state of two input pins connected to
switches and controlling an output pin connected to an LED, the NAND logic function can be
implemented entirely in software. The output of the NAND gate is LOW only when both inputs
are HIGH; otherwise, the output remains HIGH [1]. The truth table of a two-input NAND gate

Circuit Description:

The circuit consists of an ATmega32 microcontroller, two SPST switches used as logic inputs,
two  pull-down  resistors  to  ensure  stable  logic  levels,  and  an  LED  connected  as  the  output
indicator. The switches are connected to digital input pins of the microcontroller, while the LED
is connected to a digital output pin through a current-limiting resistor. When the switches are
pressed  or  released,  the  microcontroller  reads  the  input  states  and  computes  the  NAND
operation, updating the LED state accordingly.

 Workings:

When the circuit is powered, the ATmega32 continuously monitors the logic levels of the two
input pins connected to the switches. These inputs represent logic ‘0’ when the switch is open
and logic ‘1’ when the switch is pressed. The microcontroller executes a NAND logic operation
in software. If both inputs are HIGH, the output pin is driven LOW, turning the LED OFF. For
all other input combinations, the output pin is driven HIGH, turning the LED ON. This behavior
confirms the correct operation of the NAND gate.

Theory:

A half-wave rectifier is an electrical circuit designed to transform alternating current (AC) into
pulsating direct current (DC) by permitting current flow during only one half of the AC cycle.
This is accomplished using a diode, which acts as a one-way switch. During the positive half-
cycle of the AC input, the diode is forward-biased, allowing current to pass through, whereas
in the negative half-cycle, it becomes reverse-biased and prevents current flow. Consequently,
only the positive half of the waveform reaches the output, while the negative half is blocked,
producing a pulsating DC output [1].

functions  as  the  rectifier,  permitting  current  flow  only  during  the  positive  half-cycle.  The

as ripples, making it less stable than a full-wave rectifier [2].

This experiment aims to observe the rectified waveform and examine its behavior in a half-

process.  Half-wave  rectifiers  are  commonly  employed  in  low-power  applications,  such  as

Experiment No.: 04
Name of the Experiment:
Observation of a Single-Phase SCR with R Load.
Objective:
1. To analyze the operation of a single-phase SCR circuit with a resistive load by observing its
voltage and current waveforms.
2. To understand the effect of varying the firing angle on the conduction period and power
delivered to the load.
3. To investigate the performance parameters of the circuit.
Theory:
A controlled single-phase SCR (Silicon Controlled Rectifier) operates by using a gate triggering pulse
to control the conduction period in an AC circuit. The phase-control thyristor remains in a non-
conducting state until a gate pulse is applied, at which point it turns on and conducts current until the
AC voltage crosses zero and the current falls below the holding level and is turned off due to natural
or line commutation. By adjusting the firing angle (the delay in triggering within each AC cycle), the
average power delivered to the load can be controlled. This principle is essential in phase-controlled
rectifiers, where partial conduction of the AC waveform allows precise voltage and power regulation.
Such control is widely used in applications like motor speed regulation, heater control, and dimming
circuits [2].
Effect of Firing Angle (α):
• For α = 0°, the circuit behaves like a normal diode rectifier.
• For α = 90° or more, the output voltage is significantly reduced, and for α ≥ 180°, no conduction
occurs.

Discussion:
In the experiment, the operation of a single-phase SCR with an R load was observed by analyzing the
voltage and current waveforms. The SCR was triggered at different firing angles, and its conduction
characteristics were examined. It was found that as the firing angle increased, the conduction period
decreased, reducing the power delivered to the load. The waveforms confirmed the expected behavior,
demonstrating phase control of the AC signal. Some minor deviations were observed due to circuit
losses and triggering inaccuracies.
Conclusion:
The principle of controlled rectification using a single-phase SCR with an R load was successfully
demonstrated. The relationship between the firing angle and power delivered to the load was verified
through waveform analysis. It was concluded that increasing the firing angle reduces the conduction
period, thereby lowering the output power. The experiment validated the theoretical concepts of SCR
phase control. Overall, the results confirmed the effectiveness of SCRs in AC power regulation
applications. This converter is not normally used in industrial applications because it has high ripple

**Theory:**

**AVR Study:** The Atmega32 is a popular 8-bit microcontroller from the AVR family manufactured by Atmel (now part of Microchip Technology). It features a rich set of peripherals and is widely used in embedded systems.

**LED Blinking:** In this experiment, the code manipulates the output on PORTC and PORTB to control LEDs connected to each pin. 4. A delay of 1 second (**\_delay\_ms(1000)**) is added between each transition for clear visualization.
